issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of fact do not bind a revisional court when they rest on conjecture or disregard uncontroverted material evidence.
material_facts: The landlady sought possession of the entire house for herself and her family and brought eviction proceedings against both tenants at the same time.

The Rent Controller and Appellate Authority treated the government accommodation as having three bedrooms, although unchallenged evidence described it as one bedroom, a store, a kitchen and a small dining room.
The authorities considered the landlady to be seeking only the hall, overlooking her evidence that she needed the entire house and had also sought eviction of the other tenant.
The authorities inferred that the landlady would not give up the rent without properly considering her evidence about her grown children and her need for the house.
The High Court reversed the concurrent findings and ordered eviction on the ground of bona fide residential need.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in disregarding the authorities’ findings because their inherent defects deprived them of binding force in revision.
issues.legal_principle: The rule against disturbing concurrent findings applies where they are findings based on facts. Findings founded on conjecture, fictitious material or a failure to consider relevant uncontroverted evidence are not binding findings of fact. The Court relied on Hiralal Vallabhram v. Sheth Kasturbhai Lalbhai and others, AIR 1967 SC 1653, and considered the landlady’s claim under section 13(3)(a)(i)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.

rule.if: rent_revision_proceeding and concurrent_findings and findings_based_on_conjecture_or_fictitious_material and relevant_uncontroverted_evidence_ignored

predicates.rent_revision_proceeding: A party seeks revision of an eviction decision made by statutory rent authorities.
predicates.concurrent_findings: The rent authorities reached the same factual conclusion.
predicates.findings_based_on_conjecture_or_fictitio: The authorities based their conclusion on assumptions or material not supported by the evidence.
predicates.relevant_uncontroverted_evidence_ignored: The authorities failed to consider evidence relevant to the conclusion that was not challenged.

issues.definition: When a revision concerns concurrent findings that rest on conjecture and disregard relevant uncontroverted evidence, the revisional court may disregard those findings.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s awareness of, or acquiescence in, use of residential premises for a non-residential purpose does not overcome the statutory restriction on conversion without written approval.
material_facts: The hall was part of a residential building and was used by the tenant, a medical practitioner, as a clinic.
The parties had not obtained the Rent Controller’s written consent to convert the residential premises to non-residential use.
The tenant relied on the landlady’s awareness of the clinic and her failure to object as showing that the hall had been let for that use.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not rely on the landlady’s awareness or lack of objection to overcome the statutory restriction on conversion.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949 prohibits conversion of a residential building into a non-residential building without the Rent Controller’s written consent. The Court relied on Kamal Arora v. Amar Singh & Ors., [1985] SCC (Supplementary) 481, and distinguished Dr. Gopal Dass Verma v. Dr. S.K. Bhardwaj & Anr., [1962] 2 SCR 678.

rule.if: residential_need_eviction_proceeding and residential_building_used_for_nonresidential_purpose and no_written_controller_consent and landlord_knew_of_use

predicates.residential_need_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction so that the premises can be used for residential occupation.
predicates.residential_building_used_for_nonresiden: The tenant uses premises in a residential building for a non-residential purpose.
predicates.no_written_controller_consent: The parties did not obtain written approval from the rent authority for the change in use.
predicates.landlord_knew_of_use: The landlord knew that the tenant was using the premises for the non-residential purpose.

issues.definition: Where residential premises are used non-residentially without written approval, the landlord’s knowledge of that use does not validate the conversion.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot obtain consideration of a late claim that premises were let for composite residential and non-residential use after having abandoned that position, where the claim raises mixed questions of fact and law.
material_facts: The tenant’s written statement said the hall was taken for both residence and use as a clinic.
When giving evidence, the tenant took the position that the hall had been let only for running a clinic.
The tenant did not raise the argument based on the amended definition of a non-residential building before the rent authorities, the High Court, or in the grounds of the special leave petition.
The argument depended on the nature of the premises’ use and ran counter to the statutory restriction on conversion without written consent.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to examine the amended-definition argument; the tenant could not revive the abandoned composite-use position, and the argument was not a pure question of law that could be raised for the first time.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law may be raised for the first time before a higher court, but a mixed question of fact and law is not thereby entitled to first-time consideration. The Court relied on Management of the State Bank of Hyderabad v. Vasudev Anant Bhide and others, AIR 1970 SC 196, and applied section 11 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949 and the amended definition in the East Punjab Rent Restriction (Chandigarh Amendment) Act, 1982. It also applied the principle that pleadings form the foundation of a party’s case and a party cannot abandon them and propound a different case.

rule.if: rent_restriction_appeal and tenant_abandoned_composite_use_position and tenant_raises_composite_use_argument_late and argument_depends_on_facts_about_use

predicates.rent_restriction_appeal: A tenant appeals in an eviction proceeding under rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_abandoned_composite_use_position: The tenant pleaded that the premises were taken for both residential and non-residential use but later maintained that they were taken only for non-residential use.
predicates.tenant_raises_composite_use_argument_lat: The tenant first relies on the composite-use position before a higher court after not raising it before the lower authorities.
predicates.argument_depends_on_facts_about_use: Resolving the argument requires determination of facts about the purpose for which the premises were let or used.

issues.definition: When a tenant abandons a composite-use position and later raises an argument that depends on facts about use, the court may decline to consider that argument in the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent eviction proceedings against different tenants do not amount to a repeated application for eviction on the ground of bona fide residential requirement merely because the landlord succeeds against one tenant and not the other.
material_facts: The landlady initiated eviction proceedings against both tenants concurrently on the ground of bona fide requirement for her occupation.
She succeeded in obtaining an eviction order against one tenant but initially failed against the other.
The proceedings concerning the second tenant continued by way of appeal and revision.
issues.conclusion: Continuing the proceedings against the second tenant did not amount to applying again for eviction on the same ground, so the second proviso to section 13(3)(a) did not bar the claim.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to section 13(3)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 did not bar the continuation of concurrently initiated proceedings against separate tenants where the landlord succeeded in one and failed in the other.

predicates.owner_requirement_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground of bona fide need for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.landlord_filed_concurrent_cases_against_: The landlord initiated eviction proceedings at the same time against different tenants occupying separate parts of a property.
predicates.landlord_succeeded_against_one_tenant_an: The landlord obtained an eviction order against one tenant but did not initially obtain one against another.

issues.definition: When a landlord simultaneously brings owner-requirement eviction cases against separate tenants, success in one and initial failure in another does not make continuation of the latter case a repeat application.
